cands.bio: Democrat and attorney who has served in the U.S. House since 2003, representing the old 38th District and now the 41st. She sits on Ways and Means and is ranking member of its Trade Subcommittee. Former labor lawyer, IBEW Local 441 compliance officer and Orange County AFL-CIO executive secretary-treasurer.

controversies.text: Federal records show $17,900 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021.
Missed 11 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (1.6%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 7, 2025-12-09 to 2025-12-10.

endorsements.text: Endorsed by U.S. Reps. Pete Aguilar and Hakeem Jeffries (2026 race).
Endorsed by the Democratic Party of California and the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO (2026 race).
Endorsed by the California Teachers Association, Equality California and the Sierra Club Angeles Chapter (2026 race).

cands.gaps: We found no documented statements or actions by Sánchez on data centers, homestead property taxes, slowing growth or land conservation, school choice or teacher pay, or police pay and pensions. Her stands on immigration and guns come from summaries and her campaign site, not from her own statements in primary sources. The Wikipedia positions section has few dates. She did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey. Her campaign site says she passed a law banning hedge funds from buying single-family homes, but the pages we read do not name the bill, so we could not confirm it. Her stand on H-1B visas was not found.

votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

qual.background: U.S. representative since 2003 and senior member of Ways and Means (tax, trade, health). Former House Ethics Committee ranking member and Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair. Earlier a labor and employment attorney (UCLA J.D. 1995), IBEW compliance officer, and executive secretary-treasurer of the Orange County AFL-CIO.
qual.why: More than two decades in the office she holds, plus a law degree and a career in labor law, fall in the high band for lawmaking, oversight and budget work.

land-for-floridians.evidence: Her campaign website says she "passed legislation to ban hedge funds from buying up single-family homes and pricing families out of the market." This is a campaign claim; the page does not name the bill.

workers-first.evidence: Voted Nay on the Laken Riley Act, which requires DHS to detain certain unlawfully present people arrested for burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting (passed the House 263-156, signed Jan. 29, 2025).

second-amendment.evidence: Wikipedia's summary of her record says she supports gun control, including background checks, no-fly-no-buy, closing the gun show loophole, and liability for gun makers and sellers.

pro-life.evidence: Has voted against many anti-abortion bills, including the Child Interstate Abortion Notification Act and bills barring federal funding of abortion, and strongly opposed the Protect Life Act in 2011.

cands.name: Mitch Clemmons

money.note: Individuals gave $5,454; PAC money $200; candidate's own money $500. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Plumber and small-business owner who has run a plumbing company since 2002, after working as a warehouse manager for Lantis Eyewear. He studied aerospace engineering technology at Cal Poly Pomona. Republican candidate for U.S. House in District 41 in 2026. He lost the 2022 race for state Senate District 30.

endorsements.text: Listed in his own Ballotpedia survey as endorsing him: the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Assembly member Carl DeMaio, and Capt. Seth Keshel (self-reported).
Ballotpedia lists Reform California and several voter guides or recommendations, including The Morning Answer with Jennifer Horn, as endorsing him.

cands.gaps: We could not find where Clemmons was born or raised, or when he moved to California. The pages say he attended Santa Fe High School but not which one or where. He has held no elected office, so there is no legislative record. We found no stated positions on data centers, homestead property taxes, foreign or institutional land buying, growth and land protection, H-1B or immigration enforcement specifics, guns, or abortion. His campaign website names priorities (housing affordability, small business, public safety) but gives no detailed policy statements. His account of how long he has run his plumbing business varies between sources (since 2002 versus about 30 years).

score.why: Raised $6,154, under $50,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.
score.why_money: Raised $6,154, under $50,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

qual.background: Has owned and operated a plumbing contracting company since 2002, and earlier managed a warehouse at Lantis Eyewear. He has held no elected or appointed office, and lost the 2022 state Senate District 30 race.
qual.why: Business ownership and management fit the middle band for this office. There is no legislative, legal, or policy record, so he scores at the low end of that band.
qual.label: Business ownership and management fit the middle band for this office. There is no legislative, legal, or policy record, so he scores at the low end of that band.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: In his 2022 Ballotpedia survey (state Senate race), he said he is a proponent of school choice so parents can send their children to the school that will serve them best. He did not mention teacher pay.

back-police-order.evidence: In his 2026 Ballotpedia survey he said he wants to restore law and order, including cracking down early on small crimes while treating homelessness humanely.
